Apple___Apple_scab.description: Apple scab is one of the most economically important diseases of apple worldwide. It is caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis and can cause severe defoliation and fruit loss if left untreated.
symptoms: Olive-green to black velvety lesions on leaves
Lesions on both upper and lower leaf surfaces
Infected leaves may turn yellow and drop prematurely
Scabby, cracked, or distorted fruit with dark spots
Reduced fruit size and marketability
Cork-like texture on affected fruit areas
causes: Caused by the fungus Venturia inaequalis
Overwinters in infected fallen leaves
Ascospores released during wet spring weather
Spreads via rain splash and wind
Favored by cool, moist weather (13–24°C)
treatment: Apply fungicides (captan, myclobutanil, or mancozeb) at bud-break
Follow a spray program every 7–14 days during wet weather
Remove and destroy fallen infected leaves
Prune trees to improve air circulation
Use sterol-inhibiting fungicides for curative action within 72 hours of infection
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties (e.g., Liberty, Freedom, Enterprise)
Rake and destroy fallen leaves each autumn
Maintain good orchard sanitation
Ensure adequate spacing for air circulation
Monitor local disease forecast services for spray timing

Apple___Black_rot.description: Black rot is a serious fungal disease that affects apples, causing fruit rot, leaf spots (frog-eye leaf spot), and cankers on branches. It is caused by Botryosphaeria obtusa and can lead to significant yield losses.
symptoms: Circular brown lesions with purple borders on leaves (frog-eye leaf spot)
Fruit rot beginning at the calyx end, turning black
Mummified black fruits that remain on the tree
Reddish-brown cankers on branches and trunks
Premature leaf drop in severe infections
Black pycnidia (fungal fruiting bodies) visible on cankers
causes: Caused by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa
Overwinters in mummified fruit and infected bark
Spores spread by rain and wind
Enters through wounds, pruning cuts, or natural openings
Warm, wet weather (21–30°C) promotes disease development
treatment: Remove and destroy all mummified fruits and dead wood
Apply fungicides containing captan, thiophanate-methyl, or ziram
Prune out infected branches well below canker margins
Treat pruning wounds with appropriate protective fungicide
Spray schedule every 10–14 days from petal fall through harvest
prevention: Maintain vigorous tree health through balanced fertilization
Remove all mummified fruits and debris after harvest
Avoid tree wounds that allow fungal entry
Select resistant varieties where available
Implement a full-season spray program in high-risk areas

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: Cedar apple rust is a fungal disease requiring two host plants — Eastern red cedar (Juniperus virginiana) and apple — to complete its life cycle. It causes bright orange spots on apple leaves and fruit.
symptoms: Bright orange-yellow spots on upper leaf surface in spring
Tube-like structures (aecia) on lower leaf surface
Premature defoliation in heavy infections
Orange lesions on fruit and fruit stems
Distorted or cracked fruit surface
Raised, spore-bearing tubes visible on undersides of leaves
causes: Caused by the fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae
Requires both cedar/juniper and apple to complete life cycle
Orange gelatinous galls form on cedars after spring rain
Wind carries spores from cedars to apples in spring
Infection occurs in cool, moist conditions
treatment: Apply fungicides (myclobutanil, propiconazole) from pink bud through 2–3 weeks after petal fall
Remove cedar galls before they release spores
Protective sprays timed with cedar spore release
Remove nearby Juniperus hosts if feasible
Use systemic fungicides for curative action
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties (e.g., Redfree, Williams Pride)
Remove Eastern red cedars within 1–2 miles if possible
Begin protective spray programs in early spring
Scout for orange gelatinous galls on cedars as a warning signal
Maintain tree vigor through proper nutrition and irrigation

Apple___healthy.description: This apple plant appears healthy with no signs of disease or pest damage. Healthy apple leaves are smooth, deep green, and free from spots, discoloration, or abnormal growth.
symptoms: Leaves are uniformly green with no spots or lesions
No premature leaf drop or yellowing
Fruit develops normally without rot or blemish
Vigorous shoot growth and healthy branching
No visible cankers or fungal growth on bark
treatment: Continue regular monitoring for early signs of disease
Maintain balanced fertilization program
Ensure adequate irrigation during dry periods
Carry out standard pruning for airflow and light penetration
prevention: Follow an integrated pest and disease management (IPM) program
Practice good orchard sanitation
Monitor weather forecasts for disease-favorable conditions
Apply preventive sprays during high-risk periods
Maintain tree health through proper nutrition and watering

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.description: Gray leaf spot (GLS), caused by Cercospora zeae-maydis, is one of the most yield-limiting diseases of corn worldwide. It thrives under humid, warm conditions and can cause complete defoliation in severe cases.
symptoms: Rectangular, tan to gray lesions with parallel edges running between leaf veins
Lesions initially appear as small, irregular spots
Gray sporulation on lesion surface in humid conditions
Premature leaf death (blighting) in severe infections
Lesions may coalesce, killing entire leaves
Yield losses up to 50% in severe epidemics
causes: Caused by the fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis
Overwinters in infected corn residue
Spores spread by wind and splashing rain
Favored by warm (25–30°C) and humid conditions
Continuous corn or minimum tillage increases risk
Dense plant populations reduce air circulation
treatment: Apply strobilurin or triazole fungicides at or before symptom onset
Fungicide application most effective at VT to R1 (tassel to silking) stage
Use products like azoxystrobin, propiconazole, or pyraclostrobin
Multiple applications may be needed in high-pressure years
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant hybrids (most effective strategy)
Rotate crops — avoid continuous corn production
Till crop residue to reduce inoculum
Reduce plant density to improve air flow
Scout fields regularly from V6 onward during warm, humid weather

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.description: Common rust, caused by Puccinia sorghi, is widespread across corn-growing regions. While often manageable, severe infections in susceptible hybrids can cause significant yield loss, especially when infection occurs before silking.
symptoms: Small, oval to elongate powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules are brick-red to cinnamon-brown initially
Pustules turn black as the season progresses
Pustules may appear on husks and leaf sheaths
Severe infection causes yellowing and death of leaves
Premature senescence of heavily infected plants
causes: Caused by the obligate parasite Puccinia sorghi
Spores (urediniospores) spread by wind over long distances
Overwinters in tropical regions; reinfects temperate zones annually
Cool temperatures (16–23°C) with high humidity favor infection
Dew periods longer than 6 hours promote spore germination
treatment: Apply fungicides (triazoles or strobilurins) when pustules first appear
Most effective when applied before tasseling in susceptible hybrids
Products: propiconazole, azoxystrobin, tebuconazole
Economic threshold: treat when 5% or more of plants have pustules before silking
prevention: Plant rust-resistant corn hybrids
Early planting to avoid peak rust pressure in late season
Scout fields after weather events bringing cool, moist air
Monitor pustule density early for timely fungicide decisions
Avoid high nitrogen applications that favor disease spread

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: Northern leaf blight (NLB), caused by Exserohilum turcicum, is a common fungal disease of corn that can cause significant yield loss, especially when it infects the ear leaf or above during grain fill.
symptoms: Long, elliptical, cigar-shaped gray-green to tan lesions
Lesions typically 2.5–15 cm long with wavy edges
Lesions appear first on lower leaves, progressing upward
Dark sporulation visible on lesions in humid weather
In severe cases, entire plant appears gray and blighted
Early infection (before tasseling) can cause yield losses >50%
causes: Caused by the fungus Exserohilum turcicum
Overwinters in infected corn residue
Spores dispersed by wind and rain
Favored by moderate temperatures (18–27°C) and high humidity
Dew or wet conditions for 6+ hours needed for infection
No-till and reduced tillage increase inoculum levels
treatment: Apply fungicides at or before VT/R1 growth stage for best results
Effective products: azoxystrobin, propiconazole, pyraclostrobin
Two-pass programs may be warranted in high-risk environments
Scout for lesions on lower leaves from V8 stage onward
prevention: Plant hybrids with NLB resistance (Ht genes provide race-specific resistance)
Rotate corn with other crops
Deep till to bury crop residue and reduce inoculum
Avoid dense planting to improve canopy airflow
Implement early-season scouting programs

Corn_(maize)___healthy.description: This corn plant appears healthy and vigorous. Healthy corn has dark green leaves with no spots, lesions, or discoloration, and develops strong stalks with good ear formation.
symptoms: Leaves are uniformly dark green and upright
No lesions, spots, or discoloration visible
Strong, thick stalks with good standability
Robust tasseling and silking development
Good ear development and kernel fill
treatment: Continue regular scouting for early disease detection
Maintain soil health with appropriate fertilization
Ensure adequate soil moisture through irrigation
Monitor for pest pressure (aphids, corn borer)
prevention: Follow a crop rotation schedule to minimize disease pressure
Use high-quality certified seed from reputable sources
Scout fields weekly during the growing season
Optimize plant populations for your hybrid and environment
Maintain balanced soil fertility through regular testing

Potato___Early_blight.description: Early blight, caused by Alternaria solani, is a common and widespread potato disease. It typically affects older, lower leaves first and can cause significant defoliation and reduced tuber yield, especially in stressed plants.
symptoms: Dark brown to black angular lesions with concentric rings (target-board pattern)
Lesions first appear on older, lower leaves
Yellow halo may surround lesions
Premature defoliation starting from the bottom of the plant
Dark, sunken lesions may appear on tuber skin
Severely affected plants may lose 50–75% of their foliage
causes: Caused by the fungus Alternaria solani
Overwinters in infected plant debris and soil
Spread by wind, rain splash, and irrigation water
Favored by warm (24–29°C), alternating wet and dry conditions
Plant stress (nutrient deficiency, drought) increases susceptibility
Early-planted or older potato fields are most at risk
treatment: Apply fungicides (chlorothalonil, mancozeb, azoxystrobin) at first sign of disease
Begin spray programs when plants are about 15 cm tall or at first symptom
Repeat applications every 7–14 days during wet conditions
Ensure good spray coverage of lower canopy where infection starts
Tank-mix fungicides to manage resistance
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers
Rotate crops — avoid potato/tomato in the same field for 2–3 years
Maintain adequate plant nutrition, especially nitrogen
Avoid overhead irrigation; use drip irrigation where possible
Plant early-maturing or resistant varieties
Remove volunteer potato plants that harbor the pathogen

Potato___Late_blight.description: Late blight, caused by Phytophthora infestans, is the most devastating potato disease globally. It caused the Irish Potato Famine in the 1840s. Under favorable conditions, it can destroy an entire field within days if not controlled.
symptoms: Water-soaked, pale green lesions on leaves that rapidly turn brown to black
White, cottony sporulation on underside of leaves in humid conditions
Entire leaf and stem tissue collapses and turns black
Brown, firm rot on tubers that extends into the flesh
Infected tubers have a reddish-brown discoloration beneath the skin
Characteristic foul odor from infected tissues in advanced stages
causes: Caused by the oomycete Phytophthora infestans
Overwinters in infected seed tubers and volunteer plants
Spores (sporangia) spread rapidly by wind and rain
Thrives in cool (10–20°C), wet, and foggy conditions
Infections can spread throughout a field within 3–5 days
New, aggressive strains (A2 mating type) have emerged globally
treatment: Apply systemic fungicides (metalaxyl, cymoxanil) immediately at first sign of disease
Alternate with protectant fungicides (mancozeb, chlorothalonil) to manage resistance
Spray every 5–7 days during warm, wet weather
Destroy severely infected plants by cutting and removing haulm
Do not store potentially infected tubers — they will rot
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers
Plant resistant varieties (e.g., Sarpo Mira, Cara)
Scout fields daily during wet, cool weather
Use late blight forecasting tools (e.g., BlightPro, SIMCAST)
Apply preventive fungicide sprays before disease arrives in the area
Hill up potato rows to protect tubers from infected water runoff
Avoid working in fields when plants are wet to prevent spore spread

Potato___healthy.description: This potato plant appears healthy and free from disease. Healthy potato plants have dark green, upright foliage with no spots, wilting, or discoloration, and develop well-formed tubers underground.
symptoms: Leaves are uniformly dark green and turgid
No spots, lesions, yellowing, or wilting
Vigorous stem growth and branching
Flowers develop normally
Tubers are firm, smooth, and free from rot or blemish
treatment: Continue regular monitoring for disease and pest pressure
Maintain adequate soil moisture through irrigation
Hilling up soil around stems to promote tuber development
Ensure balanced fertilization with adequate potassium
prevention: Always use certified seed potatoes from reputable suppliers
Rotate crops on a 3–4 year cycle
Scout for late blight signs after any period of wet, cool weather
Maintain field hygiene by removing volunteer plants
Apply preventive fungicide sprays in high-risk climates during growing season
